terms.definition: Text changes made by fixed rules and word lists, without asking a language model. Here it means the existing saved version of the OCR after those rules; it can still contain mistakes.

The particular saved model responses chosen for evaluation or for a proposed reading version. Other responses, failed attempts and alternatives remain saved; selection alone does not mean a person has approved them.
A correction needed to restore the actual wording or meaning, such as a wrong name, number, missing phrase or negation. Merely changing spacing or appearance does not count.
Test examples deliberately given missing or unrelated source evidence, to check that the model asks for review instead of guessing. They are tests of behavior, not ordinary historical passages.
New serious errors introduced by cleanup into text that was previously correct, such as changing a person, amount, date, bill number or the word “not.”
Optical character recognition: software that turns a scanned page into searchable text. Its output can misread letters, numbers and layout.
The original machine-read text, preserved exactly as collected, including its errors.
A separate, corrected version intended for reading and listening. It keeps links to the original text and scan, and does not replace them.
Supported by what the original page actually shows, with a link back to that evidence. Plausible wording alone is not enough.
A record of what a reviewer can read in the scan, prepared before looking at the new model answers. Unclear readings stay unresolved.
A saved collection of the exact passages, context, image references and settings to be used in a test.
Save a fixed, identifiable version before a test so that all models use the same material and later changes are visible.
A file or text fingerprint. Matching fingerprints show that the bytes match the recorded version; they do not prove that the historical text is correct.
Changes to the project’s published base text or accepted records. A proposed correction does not automatically change these records.
A small, limited trial used to learn whether a larger workflow is worth pursuing. It is not permission to process the whole collection.
The project’s still-open decision about whether further OCR cleanup is worth its total cost, and for which uses.
A small set chosen to reveal particular strengths and failures. Its results do not estimate the error rate of the whole collection.
Groups of examples chosen to cover different conditions, such as corpus part, document type or OCR damage.
The complete collection being studied: here, the five collected parts of the 39th Congress, first session.
Kept separate from examples used to develop or adjust the method, so a later test is less influenced by prior tuning.
A few examples used to clarify how a person or method should judge cases. They are not automatically an independent final test.
Comparison examples used to check behavior, including unchanged text or deliberately missing evidence. Their exact purpose should be stated.
Text-to-speech: software that reads text aloud. Checking the text for likely spoken errors is different from actually listening to generated audio.
Retrieval-augmented generation: an AI system first finds passages, then uses them as evidence when answering a question.
Finding relevant passages in the collection, using words, meaning or filters.
Adding proposed information to passages, such as a speaker, date, subject or bill reference. Each claim needs its own evidence.
How closely the proposed reading preserves what the original scan says, including names, numbers and qualifications.
Changes to actual wording or meaning that the supplied source evidence does not justify.
Whether the reading preserves meaning-bearing details such as names, numbers, dates, negations and whole sentences. A serious change in any of these is a critical error.
A person examines the passage and source to resolve an uncertainty or check a proposed change.
The service or local software that runs a language model and returns its response.
Running a model on an input to generate a response. It does not mean the response has been verified.
Individual requests sent to a model, including ones that fail or time out. A retry is another attempt.
The pieces of text a model reads or writes, often words or parts of words. Token limits are not the same as word limits.
Surrounding text and other information supplied with a passage. It can help interpretation but must not be used to invent missing wording.
The pieces of text the model is allowed to generate in its reply.
A request that has not completed within the allowed time. It may require checking whether the model is still working.
Text cut off because an input or reply exceeds a limit. A cut-off reply is not a complete successful result.
Tests that saved work can be recovered after an interruption without losing results or accidentally repeating requests.
Continue from saved work after stopping, reusing completed compatible results rather than starting over.
Reproduce a saved transformation or result from the same recorded inputs, without asking a model again.
Saved material that can be reused when its inputs and settings still match.
A small image cut from an original scanned page. Its recorded page and position connect it to the text being checked.
Exact references connecting a claim or correction to its original passage, page and image region.
Recorded changes containing the old text, replacement text and exact location. They allow checking and reversing a correction.
The required structure and fields of a saved record or model reply. Passing this check shows correct structure, not historical correctness.
Automatic checks that data follows required rules, such as correct fields and matching source text. These checks alone do not establish historical truth.
A further test on fresh examples after choosing a method, to see whether its apparent benefit holds up.
The agreed limits on local model requests, running time, image transfers and other computer resources.
The existing version used for comparison, such as raw OCR or current static cleanup.
The extra useful improvement over the existing comparison version, after accounting for new mistakes and added effort.
A result for which the available evidence does not support a reliable answer. It is not a correct reading or permission to guess.
Explicitly declining to supply an unsupported reading or assignment and leaving it for review.
How much material the workflow completes in a measured amount of time, including the stated failures and overhead.
The actual historical passages in the test, counted once per passage. Artificial missing-image or wrong-image tests are counted separately.
A working proposal or judgment that may change after review or more evidence. It has not been adopted as a final standard.
A software connection that lets the workflow send a request to a model service and receive its response.
The program that sends the prepared requests, saves replies and tracks progress, failures and time limits.
Checks completed before a run begins, such as confirming the inputs fit the model limits and the source fingerprints match.
A coordination mechanism that allows only one participating local model request at a time, to prevent jobs from overlapping.
One request runs at a time; the next starts only after the previous request has finished or been reconciled.
A fixed set of examples and scoring rules used to compare methods. A small benchmark does not establish performance for every passage.
Words such as “not” or “never” that reverse or limit a statement. Losing one can change the historical meaning.
Using a proposed result without checking that individual result by hand. The pilot does not itself permit this for the corpus.
The pieces of text the model can take into account, including instructions, surrounding passages and the space needed for a reply.
Shortened forms such as “Mr.” or “Sec.” Preserving them avoids silently adding wording that is not printed.
